index.metaTitle: WebBrain Research — small, open models for browser agents
index.metaDescription: WebBrain’s open research: tiny models that see, decide and act in the browser, open-source ternary compression with OpenBonsai, and frozen public benchmarks.
index.title: Small models that see, decide and act in your browser.
lede: A browser agent shouldn’t need a datacenter. We build small, specialized models that run where the page is, shrink strong ones until they fit, and test every model we can find on the same frozen browser tasks.
Everything here is open: the weights and datasets on Hugging Face, the OpenBonsai pipeline, and the benchmark results, failures included.
index.principlesTitle: Three ideas run through all of it

principles.title: Specialize, then shrink
principles.body: A 2B model trained for one job can match a model ten times its size at that job. Compass Tiny v2 sits one strict match behind Qwen3.8-27B at routing; WebBrain VL 2 beats Gemma 4 E4B on strict screenshot reading at 450M.

principles.title: Run where the page is
principles.body: Vision, decisions and routing run inside the browser through WebGPU and ONNX, so screenshots and page content stay on your computer and the agent keeps working offline.

principles.title: Measure in public
principles.body: Every model faces the same frozen prompts and screenshots, and we publish what didn’t work alongside what did, so the next model is comparable with the last.

projects.name: OpenBonsai
projects.summary: Open-source ternary quantization: any BF16 model or fine-tune becomes weights of only −1, 0 and +1. **Qwen3.5-9B shrinks from ~18 GB to ~2 GB.**

page.lede: An Apache-2.0 pipeline that compresses dense language models to ternary weights {−1, 0, +1} in the Bonsai (PTQ1_0) format, so a capable model fits on the device that runs the browser. Compatible with Prism ML’s Ternary Bonsai runtime, whose own compression pipeline is closed.
page.why: There are two ways to get a capable model inside the browser: train a tiny one, or shrink a strong one. OpenBonsai is the second route, done in the open, so anyone can compress their own fine-tune instead of waiting for someone else’s release.

sections.heading: How it works
paragraphs: `openbonsai run` turns a BF16 model into a PTQ1_0 GGUF in four stages: **Rotate**, **Round** (sequential GPTQ), **Refine** (ScaleQ/CAT-Q, research only and skipped by default) and **Distill**. Calibration uses the model’s own answers to math and code prompts, following ScaleQ-1.58 (Wang et al., Intel Labs China).

The same pipeline compressed Qwen3-8B with no architecture-specific code, and the output drops into Prism ML’s llama.cpp fork. Your own merged fine-tune can be compressed the same way, using its answers as calibration and distillation data.

sections.heading: Ternary inside the browser
paragraphs: WebBrain also converted Prism ML’s Ternary Bonsai 2 vision models to ONNX for WebGPU. The first graph took minutes per prompt because prefill ran token by token on the CPU (about 0.13 s per prompt token for 2B on an RTX 5090); the rewritten graph handles 1k prompt tokens in 1.3 s and 4k in 3.3 s.
Ternary models are disabled as WebBrain’s decision provider for now, because they gave confident false answers.

results.title: Results so far (Qwen3.5-9B)
results.note: From OpenBonsai’s PyTorch harness, not Prism’s runtime. The HumanEval figure is probably optimistic: the setting was chosen from four runs on the same 50 problems. With thinking on: 32/50 and 14/25 for OpenBonsai, 46/50 and 24/25 for Prism’s model.

caveats: A research preview, not a finished product, with a measurable quality gap to the uncompressed base and to Prism ML’s releases.
Code and non-English output are still the main weakness.
Independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Prism ML. Bonsai is Prism ML’s product.

projects.name: Compass VLD
projects.summary: One 2B model that sees the screenshot, reads the request and decides. Compass VLD v6 puts vision, language and decisions in a single checkpoint that runs in the browser.

stats.label: strict browser-vision passes, best of the small models tested

page.lede: Compass VLD v6 2B reads screenshots, answers questions about the page, picks the next browser tool and answers decision questions such as “is the task done?”. One checkpoint does the work of a captioner, a planner and a judge, and it is built to run in the browser.
page.why: Every extra model is another download, another wait and another place for an agent to go wrong. One small model that can see, talk and decide is what makes a capable agent practical on an ordinary computer.

stats.label: strict passes on 100 frozen browser screenshots (90.2% rubric)
d1 page-state checks, 0 of 48 false completions
compact routing, loose match, with zero anti-patterns
per screenshot on an RTX 5060 Ti (BF16, llama.cpp)

sections.heading: What v6 is
paragraphs: **Compass VLD v6 2B** fine-tunes LFM3-VLD-2B Multipass, WebBrain’s adaptation of Liquid’s LFM3-VL-2B. It trained on 70,717 reviewed rows, with 1,631 more held out for validation:

46,879 browser screenshots with six-section descriptions (WebSight, ScreenParse, MiniWoB++ and synthetic renders) and 5,880 more from a curated set, 7,236 d1 page-state decisions, 6,950 tool-routing turns and 3,822 multilingual in-browser chats, at least a fifth of them in Turkish.

sections.heading: Three jobs in one checkpoint
paragraphs: **Seeing.** It describes a viewport in WebBrain’s six sections: page purpose, visible text, inputs, state signals, blockers and unknowns. 99.0% of its answers on 500 held-out screenshots keep that format.

**Deciding.** Questions like “is the task done?” are scored from the gap between its Yes and No logits, plus a small linear probe on its last hidden state. On the d1 final test it gets 122 of 126 checks right, confirms all 24 completed tasks, marks all 24 unknown cases as unknown and calls none of the 48 unfinished tasks done.

**Talking.** It answers from the page or from offline Wikipedia passages and cites every source it uses. It replies in the visitor’s language 96% of the time and turns down requests to act on the page, which belong to bigger models.

sections.heading: Against v5 and its base
paragraphs: Fine-tuning took the LFM3-VLD-2B base from 4 to 66 strict passes on the vision suite. On compact routing, v6 matches the right tool family in 38 of 89 scenarios against 32 for Compass VLD Tiny v5, and drops v5’s 8 anti-patterns (loops on bad URLs, refetching stale trees) to none.
**Compass VLD Tiny v5**, the previous version, is a 1.55B fine-tune of OpenBMB MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B and remains available.

sections.heading: Running it
paragraphs: For the browser there is an ONNX build for WebGPU: a 1.31 GB q4f16 or 1.96 GB q8f16 decoder plus a 379 MB vision encoder, with the decision probe in JavaScript. For desktops there are GGUF files from BF16 (3.46 GB) to Q4_K_M; at BF16 the model and its cache use under 4 GB of VRAM, process prompts at about 3,650 tokens/s and generate 100–128 tokens/s on an RTX 5060 Ti.

results.title: 100 frozen browser screenshots
results.note: Same screenshots, production prompt and regex rubric for every model; hardware and precision differ. v6 ran BF16 on llama.cpp (RTX 5060 Ti), the Qwen 3.5 and Gemma models 4-bit on MLX, WebBrain VL 2 in ONNX/WebGPU.

caveats: These are WebBrain’s own frozen suites, not general benchmarks.
Latencies are from llama.cpp on a desktop GPU; in the browser, speed depends on the computer’s GPU.
Routing’s strict exact-action score stays low (7 of 89); v6 leads on the looser tool-family match.

projects.name: WebBrain Compass
projects.summary: Small fine-tunes that pick the next browser tool and its arguments, so routine steps don’t need a large planner.

stats.label: strict routing matches /89, Tiny v2 vs its base

page.lede: Models of about 2–4B parameters trained to choose WebBrain’s next browser tool and its arguments in Compact mode: answer, ask for clarification, make a grounded tool call, or escalate. Plus a free hosted route, WebBrain Compass 1.0.
page.why: Most steps in a browser task are routine: read the page, click the right button. A small router that gets those right lets the big model do only the hard parts, and lets routing run on the edge or the device.

sections.heading: The models
paragraphs: **Compass Tiny v1** (2.6B, from LiquidAI LFM2.5-2.6B) matched Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on expected tool names: 42/89, against 34 for its base and 12 for Qwen3.5-9B.

**Compass Tiny v2** is a LoRA fine-tune of OpenBMB MiniCPM5-2B, trained for one epoch on 7,311 reviewed examples. It doubled its base on strict routing (9 → 16 of 89) and loose routing (21 → 41), one strict match behind Qwen3.8-27B (17/89) at roughly one-tenth the parameters.
**Compass Tiny XS v3** moves to the 1.7B Spark-X2.5 base, with ONNX builds for the browser.

sections.heading: WebBrain Compass 1.0 (hosted)
paragraphs: Launched on June 19, 2026 as a free, request-limited route so anyone can try WebBrain without a local model or an API key. On the frozen 100-case planner benchmark it reaches a 73.0% Sonnet match for $0.12 a run; MiniMax M3 scores 75.0% for $1.06.

results.title: Compact routing, 89 scored scenarios
results.note: Strict: reference tool and arguments match. Loose: tool family or name. These are routing metrics, not end-to-end success, and the Sonnet-authored reference is “a regression target, not an oracle.”

caveats: Tiny v2 kept one malformed-XML response and missed its loose target (41 against 43), so it remains experimental.
Backends, precision and concurrency differ between rows, so speeds are not controlled.

projects.name: WebBrain VL
projects.summary: A 450M vision model that turns a screenshot into what a planner needs: text, inputs, state, blockers. Screenshots stay on your computer.

page.lede: Liquid’s LFM2.5-VL-450M, fine-tuned to turn a 1280×720 viewport into WebBrain’s six-section observation: purpose, exact visible text, inputs, state signals, blockers and unknowns. It runs inside the extension through ONNX and WebGPU.
page.why: A cheap text-only planner can’t see a page. WebBrain VL gives it local eyes without sending screenshots anywhere, and it is now WebBrain’s default local vision model.

stats.label: package that runs in the browser

sections.heading: Training
paragraphs: LoRA rank 16 on a 452,847,616-parameter base, training about 0.91% of the weights, for one epoch on a single RTX 4090. Round 1 used 16,646 screenshots from WebSight, MiniWoB++ and ScreenParse; round 2 grew to exactly **50,000** by adding 33,354 synthetic HTML/CSS screens rendered in a real browser. Teacher labels came mainly from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.

results.title: 100 held-out browser screenshots
results.note: Task-specific parity, not universal superiority: Qwen and Gemma keep higher mean scores. The ONNX build’s gain over PyTorch (44 vs 36) is a runtime effect.

caveats: Teacher labels may contain OCR errors or hallucinations; high-impact visual claims should be corroborated.

projects.name: d1 decisions
projects.summary: A model that doesn’t write text at all: it answers yes/no and multiple-choice questions about the page, like “is the cart ready?”, in one pass on WebGPU.

page.lede: An on-device decision provider built from LiquidAI’s d1-omni-600M. It generates no tokens: given bounded page state and screenshots, it returns a choice, a probability of yes, or an ordinal score.
page.why: Many agent steps are really questions with a few possible answers. Answering them with probabilities instead of generated text is faster, and a calibrated “I’m not sure” is safer than a confident guess.

stats.label: decisions match FP32, max probability gap 0.010

sections.heading: How it runs
paragraphs: A bidirectional encoder with six full-attention layers, served in the browser through WebGPU (hardware WebGPU with buffer limits of at least 128 MiB). The browser build stores FP16 weights and computes in FP32; against the FP32 release it agrees on all 144 test decisions, with a largest probability difference of 0.010.
d1 page-state data also trains Compass VLD, which now takes priority for automatic decisions once it is downloaded.

caveats: Experimental, and optional in WebBrain’s settings.
No blog post covers d1 yet; these details come from WebBrain’s model documentation.

projects.name: Open benchmarks
projects.summary: Frozen, public tests of which models can actually drive a browser: 100 planner prompts, 100 vision screenshots, compact routing, all with failures published.

page.lede: Benchmarks built from WebBrain’s real work: the same 100 browser-agent prompts, frozen to one system prompt and tool schema, run against every new model, plus a 100-screenshot vision suite and a compact routing test.
page.why: Model launches come with general benchmarks, but a browser agent needs to know one thing: will this model pick the right action on a real page? Freezing the test makes every new model comparable with every old one.

stats.label: per 100 calls, cheapest strong row (Ling 3.0 Flash VL)

sections.heading: The frozen planner test
paragraphs: 100 single-turn Chrome browser-agent prompts, frozen to the May 23, 2026 Claude Sonnet 4.6 system prompt and its 41-tool schema. The runner captures the first response only and does not execute it. Scores: parsed tool calls, strict exact first call, ideal tool name, and agreement with Sonnet’s choice.
A peer-consensus variant scores each model against all the others, with no single judge: DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 leads at 51.8% for $0.050 a replay.

sections.heading: Vision
paragraphs: Each model gets 100 browser screenshots and WebBrain’s six-section vision prompt. MiMo-V2.6-Flash leads the hosted models at 81/100; among small models Compass VLD v6 2B scores 66, Qwen 3.5 4B 55 and WebBrain VL 2 450M 44.

results.title: Frozen planner test: current leaders
results.note: Reference-based and consensus scores are not ground truth. First action only: no multi-turn recovery and no executed actions. Results are dated snapshots.

caveats: Frozen-table and consensus percentages should not be mixed.
Latencies from different hosts are not controlled.

projects.name: Giving open models eyes
projects.summary: Strong text-only models can’t see a page. We attach a frozen vision tower with a small trained projector: **30.68M** new parameters give a 33B model sight.

stats.label: parameters trained to add vision to Laguna XS 2.1

page.lede: Freeze the text backbone, freeze an existing vision tower (Kimi K2.6’s MoonViT), and train only a small projector between them. WebBrain did this for Poolside’s Laguna XS 2.1 and for DeepSeek V4 Flash, and published the results.
page.why: The cheapest strong planners are often text-only, and text can’t show a canvas, a chart or an overlay covering a button. A graft adds sight for a tiny fraction of the cost of training a multimodal model.

stats.label: new parameters, Laguna XS 2.1 Vision projector

sections.heading: Laguna XS 2.1 Vision
paragraphs: Poolside’s 33B-total, 3B-active mixture-of-experts gets a frozen 416.9M-parameter MoonViT and a newly trained 30.68M-parameter projector, trained on 100,000 examples with up to 512 image tokens. In text-only planning it edges Qwen 3.6 27B on exact-action consensus (41.3% vs 38.1%), twice as fast (1.15 s vs 2.23 s median) at about a ninth of the cost per replay ($0.073 vs $0.670). Qwen still leads on exact ideal actions, 17 to 5.

sections.heading: DeepSeek V4 Flash Vision
paragraphs: The same approach adds vision to the previously text-only DeepSeek V4 Flash, released in NVFP4 and BF16, including the 0731 revision.

caveats: Laguna XS 2.1 Vision is experimental, not yet a drop-in serving release; serving integration, NVFP4 equivalence and final image-inference validation are pending. Its benchmarked rows are text-only.
Adding vision to DeepSeek V4 Flash does not change its text-only results.

projects.name: Fast local serving
projects.summary: Which formats and engines make strong models fast enough for an agent loop on your own GPU: NVFP4, EXL3, ONNX.

page.lede: WebBrain measures which quantization formats and serving engines make strong models fast enough for an interactive agent loop on consumer and workstation Blackwell GPUs, and publishes the quantized models.
page.why: An agent takes many steps per task, so seconds per step add up to minutes. Running locally only works if the model answers fast on hardware people own.

stats.label: throughput, EXL3 on SparkInfer vs ExLlamaV3
GLM-5.2 EXL3, single stream on 4× RTX PRO 6000

sections.heading: What we found
paragraphs: **NVFP4**: Qwen 3.6 27B in NVFP4 cut the median planner step from 10.2 s to 1.76 s and parsed more calls (96 vs 92 of 100), with the same 77.2% Sonnet match on tool-using cases. It is not a clean upgrade: it over-uses tools on ambiguous prompts (0/8).

**EXL3**: on SparkInfer, a vLLM fork, EXL3 files run roughly 3× faster than on ExLlamaV3. GLM-5.2 at 3.0–3.5 bits per weight on four RTX PRO 6000 cards reaches 121 tokens/s for one stream, 436 tokens/s aggregate at 8 streams, with 251K context.
GGUF stays the default for portability; EXL3 is best on owned NVIDIA hardware, and NVFP4 has its place on datacenter Blackwell.

caveats: Speeds come from different hosts and engines and are not directly comparable across posts.

projects.name: SafeSocial
projects.summary: A 13.6 MB image classifier that runs on the device and blurs social-comparison triggers on Instagram, without waking an LLM for every image.

page.lede: A multilabel image classifier that flags social-comparison triggers in Instagram images and video covers, so WebBrain can blur, hide, dim or warn. You can always reveal the image. Also available as an Android app.
page.why: Not every decision needs a large model. A narrow job like this belongs to a tiny model that runs instantly, offline and privately.

stats.label: servers: everything runs on the device
by default; you choose threshold and action

sections.heading: What it looks for
paragraphs: Eight categories: romance and jealousy, social FOMO, luxury and status, travel and lifestyle, body and beauty, achievement and success, popularity, exclusivity and access. The threshold and what happens on a match are yours to set.
On Android (Google Play: com.esokullu.safesocial) it samples video frames and offers Light, Aggressive and Custom modes, with no classification server.

caveats: Not a safety guarantee and not a clinical or moderation tool: a personal filtering aid, intentionally experimental.
No accuracy numbers have been published yet.

projects.name: Vision mode
projects.summary: Driving the browser from screenshots alone, clicking by coordinates like a person, for pages whose structure is missing or misleading.

stats.label: default for Act runs with image-capable models

page.lede: In Vision mode (“Tesla” mode), an Act run sees the tab only as screenshots, with no accessibility tree, element references or selectors, and acts by clicking, typing, scrolling and dragging at screen coordinates.
page.why: Canvases, maps, charts and custom widgets have little usable structure, and a cookie banner can cover the button the page structure says is there. Seeing what the user sees handles both.

stats.label: full screenshot to start, then only what changed
coordinate systems mapped back to the page
default for Act runs with image-capable models

sections.heading: How it stays cheap and precise
paragraphs: A run starts with one full screenshot. After that it sends only the changed region, a new full frame when most of the screen changed, or “no visible change”, and the model can zoom in. Coordinates are mapped back across retina displays, browser zoom and models that answer in 0–1000 space.

WebBrain falls back to the accessibility tree around file uploads, for workflows whose completion must be proved, when reading a whole conversation, on WhatsApp Web and Telegram, and when the model can’t take images.

caveats: Vision alone is not always enough: small local models often read text better than pixels, and long forms need precise targeting.
